title: Colorado individual income tax collections, July 2026
question: What will the Colorado Department of Revenue General Fund Collections Report first print for net individual income tax collections for July 2026, cash basis, in USD billions?
resolutionSource: Colorado Department of Revenue General Fund Collections Reports
resolutionRule: Resolve to the first Colorado Department of Revenue General Fund Collections Report value for July 2026 net individual income tax collections, cash basis, as posted in the Colorado state accounting system. Convert the agency-published dollar figure to USD billions and round to the agency's published precision; ignore later revisions or subsequent restatements after the first print.

reasoning.text: Base-rate/reference class: the annual official net individual income tax base is rising sharply into FY2026-27. Dividing official annual values by 12 gives monthly-average equivalents of 0.833, 0.929, and 1.045 billion for FY2024-25 actual, FY2025-26 estimate, and FY2026-27 forecast. That is the cleanest official recent base rate available in numeric form in this run; the CDOR page identified a July 2019-to-date workbook, but the workbook rows were not extractable from the available public page/export in the draft trace. The July 2019 and July 2020 CDOR-cited observations therefore remain useful July-specific stress evidence rather than final-resolution evidence.

Variant consistency: the resolver is net individual income tax collections on a cash basis. The CDOR and OSC source family is cash-basis monthly revenue; the LCS forecast values are net individual income tax revenue, used only to anchor the level and momentum, not as the final resolution source.

Level, momentum, one-off, and policy mechanisms: level starts near the FY2026-27 monthly average of 1.045 billion. Momentum is positive because LCS reports 4.9 percent withholding growth, 20.3 percent estimated-payment growth, and 15.0 percent cash-with-returns growth through May 2026. One-off risk is two-sided: July 2020 shows filing-deadline timing can dominate, but no comparable broad July 2026 deadline shift is in the official due-date guide. Policy effects are mixed, with OBBBA addbacks and unavailable triggered credits supporting receipts, while higher refunds and new credits pull down net collections.

Prior/update/interval: prior model is annual-run-rate persistence from the official FY2026-27 LCS net individual income tax forecast, checked against the available July-specific reference class. Historical sample values are 0.833, 0.929, and 1.045 billion official monthly-average equivalents plus July-specific stress points 0.614 and 1.760 billion. I start at the FY2026-27 monthly run rate of 12.5376 / 12 = 1.045, subtract 0.050 as a judgmental July seasonality adjustment because July is not a normal April final-payment peak and the official July 2019 value was below the annual monthly averages, subtract 0.015 for elevated refund drag, and add 0.000 net for policy because OBBBA addbacks and expanded credits point in opposite directions, giving 0.980. For this flow target, using the available public numeric history values themselves gives sigma = 0.434 billion; 1.28*sigma = 0.556 billion, so the rounded 80% interval is 0.42 to 1.54 billion.

Point calculation: 12.5376 / 12 = 1.0448; 1.0448 - 0.050 July seasonality adjustment - 0.015 refund-drag adjustment = 0.9798, rounded to 0.980 billion. Interval calculation from values 0.833, 0.929, 1.045, 0.614, and 1.760 gives mean 1.036 and sample sigma = 0.434; 1.28*sigma = 1.28*0.434 = 0.556. Using point 0.980 and rounded half-width 0.56 gives 0.980 - 0.56 = 0.420 and 0.980 + 0.56 = 1.540.

Counter-consideration: upside risk would land above the interval if July captures unusually large late final payments or estimated payments after the strong spring filing season, or if OBBBA conformity raises Colorado taxable income faster than forecast. Downside risk would land below the interval if refunds stay unusually elevated, high-income final payments were front-loaded before July, or weaker labor-market withholding offsets the annual forecast upgrade. An outside the interval low would be especially plausible if the first print nets a large refund-processing batch into July.

Review disposition: accepted the critique that the original interval was too narrow for a monthly cash-flow target and widened it using the available public numeric history values themselves. I also accepted the need to label the July adjustment as judgmental because extractable official CDOR workbook rows beyond the two cited July stress points were not available in the draft trace; I kept the ledger resolution date and noted it as operational.
